title: Foundations of Nursing Practice: Skin Integrity & Wound Care
html:
Skin is a protective barrier, a sensory organ, and a visible source of clinical information. Nursing care protects intact skin, detects breakdown early, supports wound healing, prevents infection, and preserves comfort and dignity. The RN assesses the whole person—mobility, perfusion, nutrition, hydration, sensation, moisture, devices, medications, and ability to reposition—not just the visible wound.

Learning goals

  • Identify common risk factors for impaired skin integrity and pressure injury.
  • Perform a focused skin and wound assessment using objective language.
  • Describe wound drainage and periwound findings accurately.
  • Use clean and aseptic principles safely during routine wound care.
  • Recognize wound findings that require prompt escalation.

Protect the skin before it breaks down

Reduced mobility, impaired sensation, poor perfusion, edema, moisture or incontinence, friction, shear, malnutrition, dehydration, medical devices, and altered mental status can increase risk. Assess the skin on admission, during routine care, when the condition changes, and at the frequency set by policy. Focus on bony prominences, skin folds, the perineum, heels, and areas under removable devices.

Prevention is individualized: support the safest mobility level, reposition according to the client's condition and care plan, manage moisture, offload pressure, use approved support surfaces, avoid dragging during transfers, support nutrition and hydration as prescribed, and inspect device contact points. Do not massage persistent color change over a bony prominence; protect the area and follow the facility process.

Skin-tone–responsive assessment
Do not look for redness alone. Compare with nearby or opposite skin, assess temperature, tenderness, texture, firmness, edema, and nonblanching color change, and ask about new pain or burning.

Describe a wound, not a conclusion

At each dressing change or reassessment, document the anatomic location, suspected type or cause when known, dimensions, wound bed, edges, surrounding skin, drainage, odor, pain, and signs of infection. Use the same measurement method consistently. Describe length by width and depth in centimeters per policy; assess tunneling or undermining only when trained and authorized.

  • Serous drainage: clear, thin, watery fluid.
  • Sanguineous drainage: fresh blood.
  • Serosanguineous drainage: thin drainage containing a small amount of blood.
  • Purulent drainage: thick, opaque drainage that may be tan, yellow, green, or brown; new purulent drainage requires prompt reporting.

Document what you observe: “2 cm × 1 cm open area at left heel with small amount of serous drainage; periwound intact and cool” is stronger than “heel wound looks better.” Objective details permit comparison over time.

Prevent contamination during wound care

Verify the order and care plan, identify the client, explain the procedure, gather supplies, manage pain as prescribed, perform hand hygiene, and select PPE for the anticipated exposure. Use the required clean or sterile technique for the wound and setting. Keep clean supplies separate from contaminated material; move from clean to dirty; avoid touching clean supplies with contaminated gloves; remove gloves safely and perform hand hygiene. Follow the specific product and institutional instructions rather than improvising a dressing or cleansing solution.

Recognize infection and urgent complications

Possible local infection cues include new or increasing pain, warmth, swelling, tenderness, odor, purulent drainage, worsening redness or color change, or delayed healing. Systemic cues can include fever, increasing heart or respiratory rate, new confusion, hypotension, decreasing urine output, or a general decline. Assess the client and the wound together, compare with baseline, obtain needed help, and follow the escalation process.

Wound separation, active bleeding, rapidly expanding swelling, new necrosis, or exposed tissue are not routine dressing findings. Protect the wound, assess the client for instability, avoid forcing tissue back into the body, and activate the appropriate urgent response. With evisceration, cover exposed organs with sterile gauze moistened with sterile normal saline and call for immediate assistance according to policy.

Evaluate healing and the plan

A dressing change is not the outcome. Reassess pain, drainage, wound dimensions, tissue appearance, surrounding skin, function, temperature, nutrition and hydration factors, and the client's tolerance. Healing trajectories vary by wound cause, perfusion, comorbidities, treatment, and age. Report a worsening trend or a plan that is not producing the expected response.

Clinical example

During a morning assessment, an RN finds new firmness and darkened nonblanching color over the sacrum of a client who has been unable to reposition independently. The RN compares the area with surrounding skin, asks about tenderness, reviews moisture and mobility factors, offloads pressure, updates the care plan, documents specific findings, and notifies the appropriate team member. The intervention is early because the assessment is more than a glance.
